passages.t: Samuel's death, and a fool at shearing time
passages.happening:
“When Samuel died, all Israel gathered to mourn for him; and they buried him at his home in Ramah” (verse 1). David goes down to the wilderness.

In Maon there is a very rich man whose business is at Carmel, with a thousand goats and three thousand sheep, and it is shearing time (verse 2). ‘His name was Nabal, and his wife’s name was Abigail’ (verse 3). She is wise and beautiful. He is harsh and evil in his dealings, a man of Caleb's clan.

David sends ten young men to greet Nabal with a wish for long life and peace. While Nabal's shepherds were near David's men, they were not harmed and nothing of theirs went missing. Now it is a feast day, and David asks Nabal to give whatever he can ‘to your servants and to your son David’ (verses 5-8).

Nabal answers, “Who is David? Who is this son of Jesse? Many servants these days are breaking away from their masters” (verse 10). Why should he give his bread and water and meat to men from who knows where? (verse 11).

When David hears it, he says, “Strap on your swords!” About four hundred men go with him, and two hundred stay with the supplies (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The chapter opens with a death that closes an era. Samuel, the last judge and the prophet who anointed both Saul and David, is buried in his own town, and the story goes on without him.

These are the years when David was an outlaw in the southern wilderness of Judah with about six hundred men, probably late in Saul's reign. In this chapter Maon and Carmel are small towns in the hill country south of Hebron, not Mount Carmel on the northern coast. The Wilderness of Paran lies far to the south in Sinai, and the Greek translation reads Maon in verse 1, which many scholars think fits better.

Nabal was a Calebite, of the clan descended from Caleb, who had received Hebron as his share in Joshua's day. The Calebites were the leading clan in exactly the area where David was living.

Sheep-shearing was a festival in the herdsman's year, a time of feasting and generosity. David's request comes on a day of plenty, and it rests on a real service. His men had camped near Nabal's herdsmen in open country where raiders roamed, and they protected them. In that world protection given was expected to be repaid with a gift. David's greeting is courteous, even calling himself Nabal's son.

Nabal's answer is a calculated insult. By asking who David is, and hinting that he is a runaway slave, he denies him any standing at all.

The chapter sits between two scenes in which David spares Saul's life. In chapter 24 David held himself back. In this chapter someone else will have to hold him back.
passages.later:
Sheep-shearing appears elsewhere as a time of feasting, as when Judah went up to his shearers (Genesis 38:12).

Proverbs warns against the trap David nearly fell into: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him” (Proverbs 26:4).
passages.asks: Nabal repaid real kindness with an insult. Ask whether you have received help that you never acknowledged. And ask how you respond when your own kindness is scorned: with a sword, or with something else.

passages.happening:
One of Nabal's young men tells Abigail what has happened. David's men were good to them. ‘They were a wall around us, both day and night’ (verse 16). Now disaster hangs over the whole household, and no one can speak to Nabal (verse 17).

Abigail hurries. She loads donkeys with two hundred loaves, two skins of wine, five sheep ready to cook, roasted grain, raisins and two hundred cakes of figs, and sends them ahead. She does not tell her husband (verses 18-19).

David has just been saying that he guarded everything of Nabal's for nothing, and that Nabal has repaid him evil for good (verse 21). He has sworn that by morning he will not leave one of Nabal's men alive (verse 22).

Abigail meets him in a ravine. She gets down, falls on her face and asks that the blame fall on her (verses 23-24). “My lord should pay no attention to this scoundrel Nabal, for he lives up to his name: His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him” (verse 25). The LORD has held David back from bloodshed and from avenging himself with his own hand (verse 26). ‘For the LORD will surely make a lasting dynasty for my lord, because he fights the LORD’s battles’ (verse 28). David's life will be ‘bound securely by the LORD your God in the bundle of the living’ (verse 29). When the LORD makes him ruler over Israel, he will have no remorse over needless bloodshed (verses 30-31).

David answers that the LORD sent her to meet him, and that her good sense has kept him from bloodshed and from avenging himself by his own hand (verses 32-33). Had she not come, no male of Nabal's household would have been left alive by morning (verse 34). He accepts her gift. “Go home in peace. See, I have heeded your voice and granted your request” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Abigail's speech is the longest by a woman in the books of Samuel. It moves from apology, to God's ways, to prophecy. She names Nabal's folly. She calls David's planned revenge bloodshed that the LORD has kept him from. And she speaks of the lasting house the LORD will give him.

The narrator plays on names. Nabal means fool, and Abigail says so outright. The word for folly is a strong one in the Old Testament. It is used for disgraceful acts and for contempt toward God, not for mere silliness.

Her gift is large, the food of a feast. Her posture is that of someone pleading before a ruler.

The picture of a life bound up in the bundle of the living comes from tying valuables in a pouch to keep them safe. God will keep David as a treasure. Its opposite, enemies flung away like stones from a sling, would have made anyone who knew the story of Goliath smile.

Blood is the key word: three times the chapter speaks of the bloodshed Abigail keeps David from. In Israel's law, innocent blood brought guilt on whoever shed it. A king who came to the throne with such blood on his hands would carry that guilt into his reign. Abigail is protecting the future king from himself.

Abigail is one of several in these chapters who say aloud that David will rule: Jonathan said it, and Saul himself.
passages.later:
Abigail's words about a lasting house look ahead to God's promise to David: “Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16).

The law left vengeance to God: ‘Vengeance is Mine; I will repay’ (Deuteronomy 32:35). And Proverbs gives Abigail's way in a line: ‘A gentle answer turns away wrath’ (Proverbs 15:1).
passages.hard:
Was David running a protection racket? And was his anger justified?

Some modern readers see David's request as a shakedown, an armed band offering protection and threatening violence when it is not paid. The text gives reasons to read it otherwise. Nabal's own servant says that David's men were a real defense and took nothing, and a gift at shearing time was customary. David's request is polite and leaves the amount to Nabal.

At the same time, the narrator does not defend what David meant to do. His oath to kill every male of Nabal's household was out of all proportion. It would have punished servants who had done nothing, which is exactly why Abigail calls it bloodshed, and why David thanks God for stopping him.

The chapter treats David's grievance as real and his planned revenge as sin. That honesty about the future king's temper is typical of the books of Samuel.
passages.asks: David was halfway to bloodshed when a wise woman met him on the road. Ask who has stood in your way when you were about to do harm, and whether you thanked God for them. And ask whether you could be that person for someone else, as Abigail was.

passages.happening:
Abigail goes home and finds Nabal holding a feast fit for a king, merry and very drunk, so she tells him nothing until morning (verse 36). In the morning, when he is sober, she tells him everything, ‘and his heart failed within him and he became like a stone’ (verse 37). ‘About ten days later, the LORD struck Nabal dead’ (verse 38).

David hears and praises the LORD, who has upheld his cause and kept him from evil, and returned Nabal's wickedness on his own head (verse 39). Then he sends to ask Abigail to be his wife. She bows and says she is ready to serve, and she goes with his messengers and becomes his wife (verses 40-42).

David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel. ‘But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David’s wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim’ (verse 44).
passages.hearers:
Nabal holds ‘a feast fit for a king’ while the real king is in the wilderness. Like Saul, he has repaid good with evil.

The LORD deals with Nabal himself. David is kept from avenging himself, and God does what David would have done wrongly. David will later say the same of Saul: the LORD will strike him down in his own time.

By marrying Abigail, the widow of a leading Calebite, David gains ties to the landowning families of the very district where he will later be crowned, at Hebron. Ahinoam came from a Jezreel in Judah, not the northern Jezreel. David's household is taking shape apart from Saul's.

The law of Moses allowed a man more than one wife. It never commanded it, and the law for kings warned against many wives. The Bible's own stories show the trouble it caused.

The last verse is short and sad. While David is in hiding, Saul gives Michal, David's wife, to another man.
passages.later:
The law for Israel's kings said, ‘He must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart go astray’ (Deuteronomy 17:17).

Later David will demand Michal back, and her second husband will follow her, ‘weeping all the way to Bahurim’ (2 Samuel 3:16).
passages.hard:
Saul gives Michal, David's wife, to another man. What does the chapter make of it?

The narrator reports it in one line. It shows Saul again treating his daughter as a piece in his quarrel with David, as when he offered her in chapter 18 hoping she would be a snare. The text gives no word from Michal. Later, when David takes her back, her second husband follows her weeping. The women and men caught in these quarrels are moved about by powerful men, and the books of Samuel record their grief without approving it.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Nabal's heart became like a stone, and God dealt with him without David's sword. Ask whether you can leave someone who has wronged you to God. And ask who in your family has been treated as a piece in someone else's quarrel, and how you could stand with them.
